Triangles as an Arrow array

Source: R/tri_arrow.R
tri_as_arrow.Rd

Write a triangle pool as an Arrow array, built with nanoarrow, in the layout of the experimental geoarrow.triangles type: each triangle is three indices into one vertex dictionary (a struct of x and y) that every triangle shares, so a vertex used by many triangles is stored once and a shared boundary is a shared index.

Usage

tri_as_arrow(x, group = NULL, layout = c("feature", "triangle"))

Arguments

x

A wkpool_tri.

group

Groups of triangles. Either one integer per triangle (a dense, 1-based group id, NA to leave a triangle out), or a data frame with columns triangle (row in x) and group, for groups that overlap (a triangle in several groups, as in an overlay). The default is the triangles' feature, or one group when the pool has no feature.

layout

"feature" (one row per group) or "triangle" (one row per triangle; group is ignored).

Value

A nanoarrow_array.

Details

With layout = "feature" (the default) each row is one group (a polygonal feature) and its value is the list of the group's triangles: List<FixedSizeList<Dictionary<int32, Coordinate>>[3]>. The list offsets are then the feature-to-triangle ranges, so an engine that evaluates ST_* per row needs no grouping column. A triangle in several groups is written in each of their rows (three more indices, no new vertices). With layout = "triangle" each row is one triangle (FixedSizeList<Dictionary<int32, Coordinate>>[3]), in pool order, the storage of the mesh itself.

Vertices are numbered by first appearance in the written triangles, and vertices no triangle uses are not written. The extension metadata holds "edges": "planar" and the pool's crs (as a string) when it has one. The geoarrow.triangles type is a draft and not part of GeoArrow; the layout may change.

See also

tri_from_arrow() to read it back.

Examples

if (requireNamespace("nanoarrow", quietly = TRUE)) {
  v <- data.frame(.vx = 1:6, x = c(0, 1, 1, 0, 2, 2), y = c(0, 0, 1, 1, 0, 1))
  tri <- new_wkpool_tri(v, vx0 = c(1, 1, 2, 2), vx1 = c(2, 3, 5, 6),
                        vx2 = c(3, 4, 6, 3), feature = c(1, 1, 2, 2))
  a <- tri_as_arrow(tri)
  a$length
  back <- tri_from_arrow(a)
  tri_measures(back$mesh, back$group)
}
#>   group area perimeter centroid_x centroid_y   point_x   point_y xmin ymin xmax
#> 1     1    1         4        0.5        0.5 0.6666667 0.3333333    0    0    1
#> 2     2    1         4        1.5        0.5 1.6666667 0.3333333    1    0    2
#>   ymax
#> 1    1
#> 2    1
